questions.explanation: 1.这位女士上周二做了什么？ A)见了计算机技术员。 C)打电话给了男士的公司。 B)将她的麻烦告诉了男士。 D)拜访了阿尔法维修公司。 [设题要点］细节信息处（Ispoketo...therelastTuesday）。 [答案精析］C。第2、3段说明女士上周曾给男士所在公司打过电话。第4段①句女士则明确表示上周二 她与男士所在公司的一位女士通过电话（there指男士所在公司），C项正确。A项利用首段的the computer technician设置干扰，但首段说明的是“女士现在正见电脑技术员”，但题干询问的是上周二的事情。B项源自 第4段②句女士所述“我当时明确说这是紧急事项，你们尽快派人来”，但由①句可知，这位女士上周二是与男 士公司的一位女性通过电话说明此信息。D项由第3段碎片信息AlphaMaintenance捏造而来，对话中只能 说明女士上周给阿尔法维修公司打了电话，并未提及女士前去拜访。

questions.explanation: 2.这位男士说他接到电话后做了什么？ A)咨询了负责人。 C)立即通知了总部。 B)尽快赶了过来。 D)指派了一名工程师来处理问题。 [设题要点］观点陈述处（AllIcantell youis...cameassoonasIcould)。 ［答案精析］B。第5段句中，男士表明"我这周接到电话后就尽快赶来了（cameassoonasIcould)”,B 项符合文意。A项由第5段①句I'mnotinchargeof(我并不负责...）过度引申而来，对话中并未提到男士咨 询了负责人。C项由第3段②句碎片信息centraloffice捏造而来，由该句整体可知真实情形为“女士给男士公 司总部打了报修电话后，总部派男士来处理女士的问题”，故应是“总部通知男士”，而非“男士通知总部”。D 项利用第3段②句中的碎片信息designatedtoyourcase设置干扰，但该内容表明“男士是被总部派来处理问 题的技术员”，而非“男士指派技术员去处理问题”。

questions.explanation: 3.这位女士周围的同事对问题的感受是什么？ A)受挫。 C)绝望。 B)吓倒。 D)惯怒。 [设题要点］观点陈述处（mymanageris...whatthefeelingisaroundhere）。 [答案精析］D。第6段②句女士先指出，她的经理因为男士拖延了这么久才来十分生气（rather indignant)，随后③句指出，虽然并不全是男士的过错，但有必要提醒他周围人对此事的态度，可见D项正确。 A项Frustration（愧恼；沮丧）B项Intimidation（吓倒；吓怕）以及C项Desperation（绝望；走投无路）由前文所 述“女士公司碰到了紧急情形，但维修人员迟迟不来”主观臆断而来，对话中均无据可依。

questions.explanation: 4.这位女士说她的经理会知道什么？ A)内容是否已被备份。 C)硬盘上存储的数据是否都已丢失。 B)他们是否能找到其他的人。 D)他们是否需要彻底清除系统目录。 【设题要点信息省略处（Mymanagerwouldknow...）。 [答案精析］A。第9段男士询问女士“电脑内容是否已备份”，第10段女士反问备份是什么，第11段男士 解释备份”的含义，第12段女士表明自己不知道，第14段女士则表示“经理会知道”，综合可知，女士的经理 会知道“电脑中的内容是否做了备份”，A项正确。B项由第4段③句女士的反问“你或者其他人就不能早点 来吗”以及第六段女士所述“我的经理对此十分愤怒”主观臆断而来，对话中并未提及经理要求换人处理问题。 C项利用第13段②句所述“否则，硬盘里存储的所有数据都会永久丢失”设置干扰，但此处为男士对维修中可 能出现情况的假设“如果不在维修电脑前进行数据备份，那数据可能永久丢失”，并非经理掌握的事实信息“硬 盘上存储的数据是否已全部丢失”。D项利用第13段①句碎片信息wipethesystemdirectoriesclean设置干 扰，但这是技术人员根据操作场景可能采取的维修操作，同样并非经理掌握的事实信息。

questions.explanation: 5.对于从事法律职业，很多人会怎么说？ A)它很枯燥乏味。 C)它很美好。 B)它很有挑战性。 D)它与大多数工作不同。 [设题要点］观点引述处（Manypeoplewillsayit'saboringfield...）。 [答案精析］A。第3段中男士首先表达自己对法律职业的观点“从事法律职业是一件很美好的事情”，后 引出其他很多人的看法“法律行业是一个枯燥乏味的行业”，题干十A项与此观点契合，故正确。B项结合常 识形成干扰，但原文中并未提及此意。C项是男士本人对从事法律职业的看法，而不是“很多人”的看法。D 项利用原文段末提及的manydifferentjobs捏造干扰，原文意在强调“法律职业工作内容的多样性”，而非强调 其“不同于大多数工作”，选项将“内部多样性”曲解为“与其他职业的差异”。

questions.explanation: 6.根据这位男士所述，他的大部分工作涉及什么？ A)在意见不合的律师之间进行仲裁。 C)购买和出售房产。 B)防止纠纷升级。 D)调解土地纠纷。 ［设题要点］人物介绍处（Mostofmyworkinvolves....）。 [答案精析】D。第5段男士回答女士的问题，介绍自己的职业是“房地产事务律师”和工作内容“主要负 责解决土地纠纷”，题干十D项契合原文，故正确。A项利用第5段的solicitor和第7段的arbitratebetween twoclashingparties混淆主体形成干扰，将纠纷主体从“有冲突的当事人（如土地所有者）”偷换为“律师”。 B项内容为第8段女士总结男士的工作内容，而非男士直接陈述的工作内容。C项干扰源自第五段Ima solicitorspecializinginrealestate，男士提及自己“是一名从事房地产事务的律师”，并非直接参与“房产买卖”。

questions.explanation: 7.为什么这位男士说，只要有可能，通常最好在法庭之外解决纠纷？ A)法庭旨在解决重大的法律纠纷。 C)法庭可能会令人沮丧且费用高昂。相说 B)法庭变得过于官僚化而无法正常运作。 D)法庭可能会令人恐惧且专制武断。 ［设题要点］原因解释处（Youneedtorememberthatcourts...）。 [答案精析]C。第9段中男士明确提到法庭像所有的官像机构一样，可能会非常混乱、令人沮丧且费用 高昂（verymessy，frustratingandexpensive）。因此，他建议尽可能在法庭之外解决问题，故C项正确。A项 将第8段女士总结男士的主要工作内容（fixpeople'slegalissues)与常识结合形成干扰，但男士并未提及法院 设立的初衷或职能。B项对第9段中出现的likeallbureaucracies断章取义，原文男士类比官像机构旨在论证 法庭可能存在的情况一—“混乱、令人沮丧且费用高昂”，并未提及法庭“过于官像化而无法正常运作”。D项 干扰源自第9段的frustrating和第7段的arbitrate，利用形近词诱导考生产生错误联想。

questions.explanation: 8.这位男士认为，任何法律专业人士都需要具备什么？ A)以独特方式提出论点的能力。 C)预见工作中任何潜在风险的技能。 B)避免相关各方产生冲突的技能。 D)清晰有力地表达自己的能力。 [设题要点］观点陈述处（andanylawprofessionalneedstobe...）。 [答案精析］D。第10段中男士提及“任何法律专业人士都需要清晰有力地阐述自己的论点”,D项是对 原文beveryeloquentatarticulatingthatargument的同义改写，故正确。A项中inauniqueway在对话中无 ，据可依。B项利用第7段的twoclashingparties和第8段的preventsaproblemfromescalating杂揉捏造干 扰，试图将男士的具体工作内容与对法律专业人士的普遍要求混淆。C项干扰源自第13段the stakesare higherincriminallaw中的stakes一词，但这句话是对刑法特征的描述，而非对法律专业人士的要求。

questions.explanation: 9.研究人员在《认知科学趋势》期刊上发表的综述中做了什么？ A)他们调查了个人既有知识与创造力之间的关系。 C)他们提出了二种针对老年人提取记忆困难现象 的解释。 B)他们提供了帮助老年人防止记忆力随年龄增长而 D)他们提出了一个有关人类信息存储与检索的新 衰退的新方法。 模型。 ［设题要点］研究主旨处（Inareview...，researchers...）。 [答案精析］C。Ⅱ段承接I段末尾所述现象“随着年龄的增长，我们中的大多数人在追忆往事时会遇到 困难”指出，研究人员在一篇发表于《认知科学趋势》期刊的综述中对这一现象为何可能发生提供了一种解释。 可见C为正确项。A项干扰源自Ⅲ段所述“个人既有知识（priorknowledge）有助于创造力（creativity）”，但这 是综述/研究的附带发现，而非其核心工作。B项虽与I段所述现象相关，但综述仅研究了这一现象的原因， 并未研究其解决办法。D项先由I、Ⅲ段中出现的stored、retrieving/retrieval捏造出“信息存储与检索”，进而 捏造出“研究人员提出了一个相关的新模型”，但文中并无相关信息。

questions.explanation: 10.多项行为学和脑成像研究表明了什么？ A)年轻人依赖记忆，而老年人则通过做笔记来提醒自己。 C)年轻人积累知识的速度比老年人快得多。 B)老年人在提取自己所需的记忆时经常会连带提取 D)老年人执行认知任务的速度通常比年轻人慢 出不相关的记忆。 得多。 [设题要点］研究发现处（...severalbehavioral andbrain imaging studieswhichshowthat...） [答案精析］B。IV段指出，多项行为学和脑成像研究表明老年人在搜索特定记忆时，往往会连带回忆起 其他不相关的记忆。可见B项正确。A、C、D项在一定程度上均是利用文中碎片字词如relyon/relymore heavilyon、accumulatedknowledge、cognitivetask与常识“年轻人记忆力好、记忆速度快、知识积累也快，记忆 力不好的老年人得靠备忘录来记事”结合捏造而出，但文中并未提及任何有关“记笔记备忘”“记忆速度”“知识 积累速度”的信息。

questions.explanation: 11.关于老年人，证据表明了什么？ A)他们展现出了保持完好、甚至时有增强的创造力。 C)他们在紧急情况下能依赖自己长期累积的智慧。 B)他们经常遭受杂乱而又密集的记忆的困扰。 D)他们可能通过遗忘既有知识而受益。 [设题要点］研究结论处（Evidencesuggeststhatolderadults show..） [答案精析］A。V段②句指出“有证据表明，老年人展现出了保持完好、甚至时有增强的创造力”，故A项 契合文意。B项借V段①句所述“这些杂乱而又密集的记忆可能带来的困难”设置干扰，但这是研究人员主要 关注的现象，并非“证据表明”的结论，且文中表述“带来的困难”中立，而选项表述“遭受困扰”偏负面。C项将 老年人决策时“能够借助他们长期累积的智慧”与文中未出现的“紧急情况”杂揉捏造，但短文中无此表述。D 项将V段末句表述老年人能“从自身既有知识中受益”反向曲解为老年人“通过遗忘既有知识而受益”。

questions.explanation: 12.从文章中我们了解到美国劳动者们的什么情况？ A)他们实际上为自己生产的商品及提供的服务感到自豪。 C)他们很少能掌控与自己工作相关的诸多事务。 B)他们担心与外部世界疏离。 D)他们渴望分享自己工作所创造的利润。 [设题要点］观点陈述处（Workersareoftennotincontrolof...fromtheirwork）。 ［答案精析］】C。Ⅱ段①句指出，工作可能会让人产生疏离感，随后②句解释原因，劳动者们无法控制自己的 工作方式、工作时间、所生产的商品和提供的服务的用途以及工作所获利润的去向，换言之，劳动者们很少能掌 控与自己工作相关的事情，C项正确。A项由段②句thegoodsandservicestheyproduce捏造而来，但文中并未 提及劳动者们对自己生产的商品以及提供的服务感到自豪。B项由Ⅱ段①句的碎片信息alienating捏造而来，错 误原因与A相似，文中仅提及客观情况“工作可能会使人产生疏离感”，并未提到劳动者们的主观看法“工人担心 与外界疏离”。D项由Ⅱ段②句所述的“劳动者们无法掌控工作所获利润的去向（whatisdonewiththeprofits madefromtheirwork)”过度引申出“劳动者们渴望分享自己创造的利润”，但在文中无据可依。

questions.explanation: 13.文章指出长时间工作会导致什么？ A)生产率的持续下降。 C)时间匮乏的感觉。 B)对身体健康的不利影响。 D)经济不平等的加剧。 [设题要点］观点陈述处（Longworkinghourscontributeto...psychologicalwell-being）。 ［答案精析］C。IV段③句指出，长时间工作会让人产生时间匮乏感，这会对心理健康产生不利影响，C项契合 文意。A项利用IV段②句productivity并结合常识设置干扰，但②句整体文意为“生产率其实一直在提高，只是劳动 者的工作时长居高不下”，并未提及“长时间工作会导致生产率持续下降”。B项将IV段③句“对心理健康 (psychologicalwell-being)的不利影响”窜改为“对身体健康(physical health)的不利影响”。D项张冠李戴，“加剧经济 不平等”为Ⅲ段中“实际工资没有跟上生产率的步伐”的后果，而非题干所问的“长时间工作”的后果。

questions.explanation: 14.根据文章所述，自动化带来了什么？ A)它改变了工作结构。 C)它将人们从枯燥繁重的劳动中解放出来。总 B)它让就业和工资受到了威胁。 D)它在IT行业创造了新的工作机会。 [设题要点］观点陈述处（Fourth，automation，.atrisk）。 [答案精析］B。V段①句指出，自动化让就业和工资都受到了威胁，B项正确。A项利用V段③句中的 changesaremadetothestructureofwork设置干扰，但忽视了句子的逻辑连接词（unless），此处为对自动化如 何才能利好于劳动者的情况假设，并非事实信息。C项利用V段②句所述设置干扰，错误原因与A项类似，同 样忽视了②③句之间通过couldintheory...Butunless...automationwillsimply...构成的“理论一现实”转 折对比关系，技术创新是本可以把人们从枯燥繁重的劳动中解放出来，但现实并没有。D项由V段③句中的 碎片信息workopportunities捏造而来，但原文并未专门提及自动化对IT行业的影响，且原文信息为“自动化 会减少工作机会”，而非“创造新的工作机会”。

questions.explanation: 15.后工作理论家主张什么？ A)在工作中寻找意义。 C)改善社区中的人际关系。 B)生活先于工作。 D)在职场中实现个人社会价值。 [设题要点］观点陈述处（Thepost-worktheoristsbelievethat...Theyassertthat...）。 [答案精析]B。И段句指出，后工作理论家认为，工作不应在我们的生活中占据核心地位，也不应占据 我们如此多的时间，③句进一步指出，尽管做一些工作可能是必要的，但人生的意义、目标和我们的社会价值 存在于在职场之外，③句总结指出，生活本身应被视为目的，换言之，后工作理论家认为生活比工作更重要， B项正确。A项由V段③句中的碎片信息meaning捏造而来，但结合③句整体可知，A项所述与原文相。 C项利用V段句的碎片信息thecommunitiesandrelationships捏造而来，但由句整体可知，后工作理论家 意在强调“维系工作之外的社区和人际关系”，而非建议“改善社区中的人际关系”。D项同样利用V段③句中 的碎片信息socialvalue设置干扰，错误原因与A项相似，与原文信息“在生活中实现个人价值”相悸。

listeningGroups.title: 短文一
transcript: When a person tries to access a memory, their brains quickly examine everything stored in it to find the relevant information. But as we age, many of us have difficulty retrieving memories.

In a review published in the journal Trends in Cognitive Sciences on February ll, researchers propose an explanation for why this might be happening: the brains of older adults allocate more space to accumulated knowledge and have more material to navigate when attempting to access memories.
While this wealth of prior knowledge can make memory retrieval challenging, the researchers say it has its upsides-this life experience can aid with creativity and decision-making.

Researchers Tarek Amer,Jordana Wynn and Lynn Hasher looked at several behavioral and brain imaging studies which show that older adults have difficulty suppressing information that is no longer relevant and that when searching for a specific memory, they often retrieve other irrelevant memories along with it. The studies also showed that when given a cognitive task, older adults rely more heavily on previous knowledge than younger adults do.

While the researchers focus primarily on the difficulties that these disorderly, crowded memories may pose, they also highlight a few situations in which these same memory patterns may be useful. "Evidence suggests that older adults show preserved, and at times enhanced, creativity as a function of enriched memories," the researchers write, They further hypothesize that older adults may be well served by their prior knowledge when it comes to decision-making, where they can pull on their accumulated wisdom.

listeningGroups.title: 短文二
transcript: There are at least four major problems with work in America today.

First,work can be alienating.Workers are often not in control of how they work, when they work,what is done with the goods and services they produce, and what is done with the profits made from their work.
Second, workers are not paid the full value of their labor. Real wages have not kept pace with productivity, driving economic inequality and a decline in labor's share of income.

Third, people are time poor. In the U. S. , full-time employees work an average of 8. 72 hours per day, despite productivity increases. Long working hours contribute to the feeling of time poverty, which has an adverse effect on psychological well-being.

Fourth, automation puts jobs and wages at risk. Technological innovation could in theory liberate people from the 40-hour workweek. But unless changes are made to the structure of work, automation will simply exert downward pressure on wages and further diminish work opportunities.

So what can be done to alleviate these problems? There are competing visions of the best way to arrive at a solution. One vision is what's known as the “post-work” position. The post-work theorists believe that work should not hold a central position in our lives or take up so much of our time, They assert that although doing some work might be necessary, meaning, purpose and social value reside in the communities and relationships built and sustained outside of the workplace.Thus, life should be seen as an end in itself.

listeningGroups.title: 讲座一
transcript: Recent studies show that self-control and persistence increase academic outcomes independent of
Q. Even our personal beliefs about effort can affect academic outcomes. Children who think effort leads to achievement outperform those who believe ability is a fixed trait.

Given the link between persistence and academic success, decisions about effort are particularly important in childhood. Yet relatively little research has explored how young children learn what's worth the effort.

We all know that infants are keen observers of the social world. But they're not just idly watching; they are tiny learning machines. They can generalize such abstract concepts as causal relationships and social roles from just a few examples. Even a 15-month-old infant can outperform a high-level computer in such tasks.

Could infants also make broad,generalizable inferences from a few examples when it comes to effort? If so, then maybe persistence isn't simply a character trait. Maybe it's flexible and adaptable based on social context.
To explore this question, we showed 15-month-old babies one of two things: an experimenter working hard to achieve two different goals, or an experimenter who effortlessly reached each goal.

Then we introduced the baby to a novel "music” toy that seemed as if it could be activated by pushing a big button on top. (The button could be pressed down but didn't actually activate anything. ) Out of sight of the babies, we turned on the music toy with a hidden button so that they heard the toy making music. We gave the babies the music toy and left the room. Then analysts, who didn't know which condition each baby was in, watched videotapes of the experiment and counted how many times babies tried to activate the toy by pressing the button.

Across one study and a preregistered duplication, babies who had seen an adult persist and succeed pushed the button about twice as many times as those who saw an adult effortlessly succeed. In other words, babies learned that effort was valuable after watching just two examples of an adult working hard and succeeding.

instead, they generalized the value of effort to a novel task. The experimenter never demonstrated pushing a button or trying to make music. Instead the babies learned from different examples of effortful actions that the new toy probably also required persistence.

listeningGroups.title: 讲座二
transcript: If chronic lateness has taken over your life and turned into a defining trait of who you are, it's likely that you're losing out on job offers, recreational opportunities, friendships and more. If you're showing up late to your own life,get organized,prioritize punctuality,and address any underlying causes.

When you have to be somewhere, try to arrive 15 to 30 minutes before you need to. If you always run late,that means you must be failing to account for something you always do. Anticipate that by giving yourself extra time to arrive. Keep track of whether or not you actually do arrive early! You might find that leaving"early"gets you to places exactly on time.

Il Set two alarms. Set one alarm that lets you know it's time to drop what you're doing, and a second alarm that means you need to walk out the door. Obey the alarms! As soon as the first alarm goes off, stop what you're doing. If it's something you'll be coming back to, like a project for work,make a note to remind yourself where you left off.Grab everything you need and make sure you know how to get where you're going. Aim to be out the door and on your way before the second alarm rings. This will only work if you take the alarms seriously, so make sure you react as soon as you hear them.

Prepare for the day ahead. Have all of your notes and materials organized well in advance of each event so that all you have to do is grab them and go when it's the actual day. If mornings are a struggle for you, do as much as you can to ready yourself the night before: before you go to bed, lay out your clothes and pack your bag for the next day.

Learn to leave time in between tasks and meetings. It soon becomes unbearable to shift between one meeting and another without a space in between. If you over schedule yourself, however, you'll arrive late as soon as you hit a bump. As well as giving you space, this time also acts as a buffer between events which can be “borrowed” from should you be held up in a prior meeting, allowing you to still get to the next one on time. Calculate transit time between activities and then add 10 to 30 minutes for unexpected delays.

transcript: Do you think Bostonians put out the welcome mat? Do you find other cities to be more or less polite? Different cities have different feels for visitors. Some are friendly and open. Some are formal and distant. Boston tends to seem hurried and sometimes a little rude. That's what some tourists have said. One study found that people here are less willing to volunteer to help strangers than those residents of other U. S. cities.

Take a close look next time you're in Boston, and here are some of the things you'll probably see: people smoking in the subway stations despite the frequent reminders not to do so; pedestrians walking when the crosswalk lights say not to do so, ignoring the cars; car drivers speeding, making a loud noise with the horn, and occasionally cursing at each other; drivers who can't be bothered to find a place to park but instead simply turn on their blinker and stop in the middle of the street.

Sometimes Bostonians seem like they're just too busy to be polite. Why is the city like that? Former U. S. Representative Chester Atkins says it's because the Puritan Founding Fathers were themselves impatient and bad-tempered and had little time for courtesy. That culture has carried down to the present day, he believes.

Boston College professor Thomas O'Connor thinks a contributing factor is Boston's history as a city where each new group of immigrants was treated with suspicion and exclusion. That's given Boston a sense of clannishness and reserve, he thinks. The idea of a stranger greeting another stranger is simply not part of the local culture, he says. People would begin a conversation with someone they know, but not with a stranger.

Ralph Whitehead, a professor of journalism at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst, thinks it's because Boston's upper class used manners to make class distinctions by being snobbish about manners. Proper Bostonians made other people scornful of courtesy, he says.

Some say that's just the way Boston is and that the city will never change. Still, other cities with reputations for worse rudeness are trying hard to change their images. Paris is one example where people are trying to be friendly. New York City is another; there, the city is trying to persuade subway riders to be more considerate.If those cities can make the effort,maybe Boston should as well.
